clue.text: Not much of an experience for the Artemis II crew at the end

definitions.text: an experience for the Artemis II crew at the end

blocks.note: the idiom for an amount so small it makes no difference to the whole

blocks.clueFragment: an experience for the Artemis II crew at the end
blocks.note: read absolutely literally: a moon capsule finishes its flight by splashing down at sea

explanation.walkthrough: Artemis II loops the Moon and comes home by splashdown, so the second half is a plain statement of fact dressed up as a cryptic.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a negligible amount, and a returning capsule ends its flight by falling into the sea, which is the same phrase read literally.

clue.text: Smiley book’s going up I learn?

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a piece told to go up is written bottom to top and arrives back to front.

blocks.note: a TOME is a weighty book, climbing the entry rather than running down it
the letter stands for itself, lifted straight out of the clue
to con a part is to learn it by heart, an old sense the grids keep alive

explanation.walkthrough: Smiley is le Carre's spymaster in the surface, which is what makes 'book' sit so naturally beside him.
explanation.definitionFit: A face built out of punctuation is what the answer names, and the smiley is the best known of them, so the definition gives the commonest member of the class.

clue.text: Insults marrow in seconds

indicators.note: Doing its literal job rather than joining two halves: one piece is lodged inside the other.

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second, and the plural asks for two of them
the nub of a matter is its marrow, the pith at the centre of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Marrow' is not the vegetable but the core of a thing, the sense preserved in 'the marrow of the argument'. Two seconds make the shell it sits in.
explanation.definitionFit: To snub somebody is to cut them dead in public, and that pointed rebuff is exactly what the plural verb 'insults' covers.

clue.text: Company actor initially wearing plain attire

indicators.note: It asks only for the letter a word starts out with, not for the word itself.
You go inside whatever you have on, so the letters doing the wearing sit within the garment word.

blocks.note: overt means open and undisguised, plain to anyone looking
Co is how company is abbreviated on any letterhead
the opening letter of actor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' is the trap: it means overt here, out in the open, rather than undecorated. The surface dresses a nervous understudy.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the heavy outer garment worn over everything else, so 'attire' names it by class: clothing, of which this is one item.

clue.text: Black, easily portable mould

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation on a pencil and on a chess score sheet
something easily portable is light to carry

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here signals a build: 'Black, easily portable' reads as one description of a suitcase, and the comma is the only sign that it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the fungal disease that rots a crop, and potato blight is one of exactly that kind, so the definition names it by family.

clue.text: Incline to quash civil act by end of day

indicators.note: To quash something is to crush it flat, and letters crushed together lose the order they were set in.
It points at the far edge of the word that follows, so only the final letter is taken.

blocks.note: the eight letters of CIVIL ACT, dealt out again
the last letter of daY

explanation.walkthrough: 'Incline' has to be read as a noun, though the surface offers it as a verb, being inclined to quash something.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the surveyor's word for a slope running upward, which is what a road's incline is: one noun plain, one technical.

clue.text: Valour shown after detonation of part of a plant

indicators.note: A blast leaves everything it touches scattered, and scattered letters do not stay in the order the clue prints them.

blocks.note: the six letters of VALOUR, blown into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is doing something unusual: it opens with 'of', which is what lets an adjective answer where a noun seems to be wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The ovule is the seed-bud inside a flower's ovary, and the answer is the adjective for whatever belongs to it.

clue.text: Tree expert’s concoction of citrus and oil-tar rub

indicators.note: A concoction is whatever comes out of stirring assorted ingredients together, and the ingredients here are letters.

blocks.note: the fifteen letters of CITRUS, OIL, TAR and RUB, stirred together

explanation.walkthrough: Fifteen letters is a lot of fodder to take on trust, so count them before committing: the four ingredients supply exactly the letters wanted, no more.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbor is Latin for tree and culture is tending, so the answer is somebody who cultivates them and the definition is the plain-English name for that trade.

clue.text: ‘Evil demon vanquished!’ makes sensational reading

indicators.note: An army vanquished is one broken up and scattered in all directions, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: the nine letters of EVIL DEMON, redealt

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark keeps the indicator inside the shouted quotation, where it reads as triumph rather than as an instruction standing outside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer was the cheap American thriller sold for ten cents, written for thrills rather than for literature.

clue.text: Sporty type beneath the surface, but one who’ll give in?

blocks.note: potholing is a sport, and it happens underground
somebody who caves in yields, and the setter makes a person out of the phrasal verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beneath the surface' is literal, not figurative: the sport happens underground. The question mark covers the second half, where a phrasal verb is squeezed into a single noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The sportsman explores caves underground, and to cave in is to yield, so one word covers both the hobby and the surrender.

clue.text: Court award presented in alternative month

indicators.note: Presenting one thing in another puts it inside, so these letters are lodged within the word that follows rather than after it.

blocks.note: or is the alternative in any either/or
Ct is how Court is abbreviated in a street address
the Order of the British Empire, the crossword's standard honour

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a prize handed over on a tennis court, and every word of it is quietly doing a different job in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names the answer by its class rather than by a synonym: it is simply one of the twelve, the tenth in the calendar.

clue.text: Astronomer’s western partner, one with a sign

blocks.note: in a western the hero's sweetheart is his gal
the Roman numeral
the lion, one of the twelve signs of the zodiac

explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' is the film genre rather than a compass point, and its hero always has a gal; 'sign' is the zodiac kind, which is the only astronomy the parse needs.
explanation.definitionFit: He turned the first telescope on Jupiter's moons and was tried for saying the Earth moves, so the definition names the man by his trade.

clue.text: Tongue-in-cheek, creep inside

indicators.note: It says the word is buried in the letters beside it, rather than describing where anyone's tongue is.

blocks.note: the run crosses a hyphen: the whole of 'in' and the front of 'cheek'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue-in-cheek' means ironic in the surface and is a hiding place in the parse. The answer sits astride a hyphen, which is exactly why the eye skips over it.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch forward is to advance by tiny degrees, and creeping is that same slow grudging movement, so the two verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: Composer of divertimento managed without it

indicators.note: Managed means contrived or arranged, and a managed thing has been put into whatever order somebody chose for it.
'Without' means lacking rather than outside, so the two letters spelling 'it' are missing from what you shuffle.

blocks.note: DIVERTIMENTO less the I and the T of 'it', leaving the ten letters that get shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: A divertimento really is a piece of music, which is what makes the fodder sit so quietly. Note that the deletion happens before the shuffle, not after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Monteverdi wrote the first great operas and eight books of madrigals, so the definition names him by his trade.

clue.text: It refreshes dictionary’s backing – and work by Bellow

indicators.note: A thing backing is travelling the other way, so the letters in front of it are written in reverse.

blocks.note: the OED is the dictionary a crossword means, turned round
to do a job is to work at it
to bellow at somebody is to rant

explanation.walkthrough: Bellow is Saul the novelist in the surface, where 'work by Bellow' is a book, and an ordinary verb in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: The spray kills the smell of sweat and leaves you feeling clean, so the definition names the product by its one job.

clue.text: Treasure’s almost buried by explosive – touching

indicators.note: It stops you a letter short of the whole word, so the last one never arrives.
Whatever buries something closes over the top of it, so one piece ends up inside the other.

blocks.note: TNT is the crossword's standard explosive, and it opens up to take the other piece
'she's an angel' is the same compliment as calling somebody a treasure

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'touching' look like the end of a sentimental sentence, and 'treasure' look like buried gold rather than a term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the line that grazes a curve at a single point without cutting it, so the definition uses the geometer's own sense of the word.

clue.text: Artist’s Power Unit and Evian Water

blocks.note: the watt is the SI unit of power
Evian is French, and water in French is eau

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are a bluff: 'Power Unit and Evian Water' reads as a delivery note, and the second half only works once Evian is read as French rather than as a brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine Watteau painted the fetes galantes of the French rococo, silk-clad parties in parkland, so the definition names him by his profession.

clue.text: Travel on board Chinook, say, seated on foam

indicators.note: It flags an example rather than a synonym: the helicopter's name is one member of the class the letters actually spell.
In a down entry, whatever is seated on something else is written above it, so this piece comes first.

blocks.note: the chinook is the warm dry wind that comes down off the Rockies
surf is the foam breaking along a shore

explanation.walkthrough: The Chinook in the surface is the twin-rotor helicopter, and 'on board' is what you are once you have climbed into one. Both readings have to go.
explanation.definitionFit: The sport is riding a sailboard driven by the wind, so the definition describes it literally: the going, and the plank you do it standing on.

clue.text: Buddy possibly needs energy to be put in goal and improved

indicators.note: It warns that the name is only one bearer of the word wanted, not a synonym for it.
Something put in goes inside, so these letters are lodged within the other piece rather than beside it.

blocks.note: the end you are working towards is your goal, and it splits to take the rest
Buddy Rich, the big-band drummer
E is the physicist's symbol for energy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a football substitution, right down to 'in goal'. Buddy is a first name rather than a pal, which is what 'possibly' quietly admits.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrich something is to make it fuller or better, and enriched flour has its vitamins put back, so the definition is the plain past-participle synonym.

clue.text: Model person appearing in NME, Time Out

indicators.note: Whatever appears in something is found inside it, so the person's letters sit within the other piece.
Read it as out of order: the letters in front of it no longer stand in the sequence they were printed in.

blocks.note: the seven letters of NME and TIME, dealt out again
bod is casual British for a person

explanation.walkthrough: Two magazine titles in italics look like one list, and the cut falls between them: Time keeps its letters while Out turns into the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the person in whom a quality takes visible form, and 'a model of patience' says exactly that, so this is the noun sense meaning exemplar.

clue.text: Elected, elevated and taken to party’s heart – then shut out

indicators.note: In a down entry an elevated piece is written bottom to top, so it arrives the other way round.
To be taken to something's heart is to end up right in the middle of it, which is where these letters go.

blocks.note: a bash is a party, and it opens up to take the other piece
a candidate who is elected is IN, and this entry climbs

explanation.walkthrough: A political career in one sentence: elected, elevated, embraced, expelled. All of it is wordplay, and none of it is the definition until the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: To send somebody away and bar their return is what the answer means, which is what shutting a person out amounts to: exile rather than a mere refusal.

clue.text: Nice woman gets a daughter into musical?

indicators.note: Literal, not joinery: the letters go inside the title rather than after it.

blocks.note: Mame, the Broadway musical of 1966
the article A, then D, the family-tree abbreviation for daughter

explanation.walkthrough: The capital N is the whole disguise: Nice is the city on the Riviera, not the adjective, and the question mark covers the leap from a place to its language.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice is French, and a woman there is addressed by the French title, so the definition asks for that word rather than for an English one.

clue.text: Child has right to enter club

indicators.note: Entering something means going inside it, so the letter is planted within the other word.

blocks.note: a bat is the club you swing at a ball
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like the sort you need the right connections to get into, which is exactly the reading the parse throws away.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoilt, badly behaved one is what the answer means, so the definition supplies the neutral word and the answer adds all the disapproval.

clue.text: Sing and entertain

blocks.note: underworld slang: a suspect who sings owns up
to entertain a doubt is to let it in and give it room

explanation.walkthrough: Two rooms in three words: the interview room where a suspect sings, and the drawing room where a host entertains. Both come down to letting something in.
explanation.definitionFit: Confessing is one sense and letting something in is the other, so the verb covers owning up and giving an idea house room alike.

clue.text: Focused on getting money – shamefaced

blocks.note: a cent is the smallest coin in a dollar
a shamefaced person goes red in the face

explanation.walkthrough: The dash hides the join: 'money' and 'shamefaced' are two separate pieces of wordplay, not one phrase about being caught with somebody else's cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean brought to a single point, one from geometry and one from a lens, so the two past participles swap straight over.

clue.text: Deceiver, foreign nobleman, featured in Observer

indicators.note: To be featured in something is to appear inside it, so one piece sits within the other.

blocks.note: one who observes is a seer
duc is the French duke, which is what 'foreign' points at

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it the Sunday paper, and the parse wants the ordinary noun instead: somebody who observes.
explanation.definitionFit: He talks a woman into bed with promises he does not mean to keep, so the definition names him by the lying rather than by the desire.

clue.text: Minister without Portfolio’s capital offence

indicators.note: It is doing its older job of lacking, not of standing outside, so the letter named simply is not there.

blocks.note: a parson is the minister of a parish
the capital letter of Portfolio is P, and P is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: Minister without Portfolio is a real cabinet post, which is what holds the surface together, and the crime really was once a capital offence. Both are bluffs.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is the crime, so the definition names it by its legal category rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Very hard as level of gratitude abroad reduced?

indicators.note: It says the word wanted is not the English one but its foreign equivalent.

blocks.note: merci is how you say thanks in France
reduced means made less

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the joke: a traveller whose thanks have run short is being called hard, and two languages end up jammed into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing no mercy is the sense, and somebody who shows none goes at you without let-up, which is the everyday way of saying it.
